To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the pathogenic transition from a benign endophytic state to the necrotrophic parasite that causes Ramularia leaf blotch disease is promoted by exposure of the host plant to abiotic stress, 2) the pathogenicity of the fungus is associated with increased levels of H2O(2) and 3) disease development is reduced in barley plants that are unable to accumulate high levels of H2(2) or that have non-functional chloroplast.

(i) abiotic stress increases the development of Ramulairia leaf spot in barley, (ii) this is associated with an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) in leaves and (iii) the pathogenic transition is not promoted by ROS, but rather is associated with changes to the host redox state.
the development of Ramu-laria leaf spot in barley is influenced by reactive oxygen species and the redox state of host cells.

reactive oxygen species are important factors in determining whether R. collo-cyni colonizes barley as a benign endosymbiont or as a necrotrophic pathogen.
the development of Ramulaira leaf spot in barley is promoted by reactive oxygen species, but the effect of this is dependent on the genotype of the host.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the transition from endophyte into pathogenicity is not a result of a senescence process, but rather is a result of factors that promote the production of reactive oxygen species in the host.
the transition of a fungus from endophytic to necrotrophic pathogen in barley seedlings is promoted by factors resulting in changes to host H2O2 accumulation.
